pages.text: The air carries an electric field even on a still day: about 130 volts a metre at the ground under a clear sky, the earth negative and the sky positive. Rain lifts it to a kilovolt a metre and a thunderstorm to ten. A roof or a cave screens it entirely.
pages.title: The Air's Electric Field

pages.text: A field mill reads it: an earthed brass vane turns over a pair of sense plates, alternately shading and baring them, and the current the field drives on and off them is amplified by an electron tube.

Dust storms are more strongly electrified than thunderstorms. Grains striking one another trade charge, the small ones coming away negative, and the field across a storm reaches tens of kilovolts a metre.

That field is not a by-product: Kok and Renno showed in 2008 that it lifts grains off the ground, so a charged storm carries far more sand than wind alone could. A field mill that reads a storm with no thunder overhead has found the sand's own charge.

So a dust storm can be quieted where its field is drained. Earth the air around a place and the sand loses the force that holds it up. Its comparator rises on a logarithmic scale, from nothing in fair weather to 15 at fifty kilovolts a metre.
